queue.tree_name: Ahuehuete del Jardin de San Fernando
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its broad crown, about 22 metres wide, inside the small Jardin de San Fernando. It stands beside, but is not part of, the separate, ticketed Panteon de San Fernando cemetery next door.
queue.story: Mexico City had protected no trees by name at all until 2025, and this was one of the first two it named. The ahuehuete in the Jardin de San Fernando went into the register at the opening of the programme, alongside a tree in Azcapotzalco, in a decree that recorded it at about 25 metres tall with a trunk 158 centimetres across. The environment department's own field sheet, from a separate visit, gives a thicker trunk and a height nearer 28 metres, with a circumference of 5.5 metres and a crown 22 metres wide. Two measuring passes, two sets of numbers, both official, and the difference tells you roughly how much precision to expect from any figure on a tree this size. It stands in a small pub
queue.name: Ahuehuete del Jardin de San Fernando

queue.tree_name: The Norfolk Island Pine of Ingle Hall
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk forking into two co-dominant leaders under a stack of horizontal branch tiers. It stands outside Ingle Hall, Macquarie and Argyle Streets.
queue.story: Asked in 2025 to name his favourite tree in Hobart, the owner of the New Town Station Nursery picked this one, and his reason was that it never changes much. Norfolk Island pines grow slowly and hold their shape, a stack of horizontal branch tiers running up a near-perfect vertical, and this one has kept its corner of Macquarie and Argyle Streets while the buildings around it got taller. The City of Hobart's register singles out its trunk: it forks into two co-dominant leaders, which on most conifers reads as a fault and on this one reads as character. It stands outside Ingle Hall, one of the oldest Georgian buildings in the city, now part of the University of Tasmania's Conservatorium of Mu
queue.name: The Norfolk Island Pine of Ingle Hall
queue.worth: closes a gap: this tree has no photograph at all

queue.tree_name: The Bhutan Cypress of Brisbane Street
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its dark green, cone-shaped column running straight up out of the footpath. It stands at 67 Brisbane Street.
queue.story: This tree is on Hobart's significant tree register for one stated reason: its loss would be detrimental to the community. Not size, not age, not rarity. The Bhutan cypress at 67 Brisbane Street earned its place as a shape, a dark green cone running straight up out of the footpath, holding a vertical line on a street that otherwise runs horizontal. It is a long way from home. Cupressus torulosa grows wild in the dry inner valleys of the Himalaya, through northern India, Nepal and Bhutan, at altitudes that hand it thin air, hard sun and freezing nights, and across that range it is the tree planted around temples and monasteries. queue.tree_name: The Dawn Redwoods of Elizabeth Street
queue.recognise: You can recognise them as three dawn redwoods within about twenty metres of each other, descendants of the 1947 seed collection that ended the species' presumed extinction. They stand on the road reserve outside 81 Elizabeth Street.
queue.story: Until 1941 this species was known only from fossils. Botanists had described Metasequoia from imprints in stone and filed it under extinct, and then living trees turned up in a valley in Hubei province, China. Every dawn redwood outside that valley descends from seed collected there in 1947 and posted around the world, which makes the three on the road reserve outside 81 Elizabeth Street the great-grandchildren of a botanical resurrection. There are three of them, within about twenty metres of each other in front of the former Commonwealth Bank building, and the City of Hobart's significant tree register treats them as a single record rather than three, because the group is the point. queue.tree_name: The Big Totara of Lillburn Monowai Road
queue.recognise: A single huge column of a trunk rising out of moss in dense wet forest, grey and red-brown bark peeling in long vertical strips, with cushions of moss climbing it.
queue.story:
A reader sent this totara from the totara trees nature walk off Lillburn Monowai Road, in the Southland hills inland from Tuatapere, with a GPS fix taken at its foot. They named it Podocarpus hallii, Hall's totara, and gave it an age of about a thousand years and a girth of 831 centimetres.

The photograph looks up the trunk from its root plate. A single column rises out of the moss, far wider than a person could reach round, its bark grey and red-brown and peeling in long vertical strips, with cushions of moss climbing it. The trunk runs straight out of the top of the frame. Around it the forest is dense, wet and green, with ferns, mossy branches and smaller trees pressing in.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the plaque on its trunk, which says plainly that a storm shortened its crown soon after planting. It stands on the harbour side of the garden.
queue.story:
A plaque on the trunk explains that this tree will never reach the grandeur of the one it replaced, because a storm damaged its crown soon after it was planted. It is an unusually honest thing for a label to say, and it is accurate.

The original Wishing Tree was a Norfolk Island pine set out from a tub around 1816, under Elizabeth Macquarie's eye. By 1905 it was over thirty metres and the most popular tree in the Royal Botanic Garden, with a custom attached: three times around it forwards, three times backwards, and then make your wish. In the 1930s it was found to be dying of old age, and a replacement was bought with money raised by the Farmer's Children's Radio Birthday Club and planted
queue.name: The Wishing Tree

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by a crown 169 feet across, held up by cables and columns, that fills a small corner park on its own. It stands in Elizabeth Ireland Poe Park at Crawford and Monroe streets.
queue.story:
Dial the number posted by the Big Oak and a camera across the street takes your picture with it. Thomasville treats this tree the way other towns treat a courthouse.

It earned that. The local history centre's curator puts its start around 1680, while admitting the date is not exact, so call it over 300 years. Its crown spreads 169 feet, it stands about 72 feet tall, and the trunk measures roughly 28 feet round; the marker says 27.5, and heights vary by source. When it joined the Live Oak Society in 1936, as the 49th member, the girth was 21 feet 6 inches.

In 1966 the city bought the corner lot outright to make a park around it, the Elizabeth Ireland Poe Park. Traffic has been the real thre
queue.name: The Big Oak
queue.worth: the tree already has one: ship this only if it is better

queue.tree_name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Balboa Park
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by a buttressed, accumulated trunk mass 12.3 metres round and aerial roots hanging from the limbs. It stands outside the north entrance of the San Diego Natural History Museum, Balboa Park.
queue.story:
This fig went into the ground as a five-gallon sapling. That was 1914, planted for the San Diego County garden exhibit at the Panama-California Exposition the year after, and it is the last plant from that exhibit still alive. A survey for the California Registry of Big Trees in 1996 put it at 24 metres tall with a crown 37 metres across and a trunk 12.3 metres round, though that last figure is a buttressed fig mass rather than one clean stem. Moreton Bay figs do not so much grow a trunk as accumulate one.

queue.recognise: The huge fig with a car-parts sculpture of Atlas appearing to hold up one long branch, a few metres from the Recoleta Cemetery gate.
queue.story: One branch of this fig reaches thirty metres out from the trunk and is over a metre thick where it leaves it. Since 2014 a sculpture of Atlas, welded from car parts by the Uruguayan artist Joaquin Arbiza Brianza, has stood underneath it appearing to take the weight. The city government calls this the oldest tree in Buenos Aires, and nobody agrees on how it got here. One account has the Recoleto friars planting it around 1718. Another credits the agronomist Martin Jose de Altolaguirre, who kept an orchard of exotic species on this ground around 1781. queue.name: The Gomero de la Recoleta

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its huge low, spreading crown, shading a quarter acre, whose branches rest on the ground rather than reaching upward, on a trunk about 7.8m round. It stands within its own fenced park on Johns Island.
queue.story:
The souvenirs say 1,500 years. The city that owns the tree says 300 to 400, and an academic estimate stretches it to 500. That gap is not carelessness, it is live oak. The species grows fast when young, slows unpredictably and rots out from the middle while the crown is still healthy, so there is no core to pull and nothing to count. What can be measured is girth, and every estimate that starts from the tree itself lands in the hundreds of years rather than the thousands.

queue.recognise: A huge river red gum with a trunk about eleven metres round, pale peeling limbs and a brown council sign naming it the Giant Red Gum.
queue.story:
On the edge of Orroroo, a small town in South Australia's northern Flinders Ranges, a river red gum stands with a trunk wide enough that a man with outstretched arms covers a fraction of it. A sign beside it, put up by the District Council of Orroroo/Carrieton, gives its circumference as 10.89 metres at 0.61 metres above the ground and its age as estimated in excess of 500 years.

Other figures disagree a little. An older sign gave about 10.4 metres, and the National Register of Big Trees records a measurement of 9.90 metres at breast height in 2009 with an age of 485 years.
